t: The picture-perfect California beach where visitors keep dying
lede: The deaths of four people and the disappearance of another in six months have raised questions about Panther beachand what can be done to keep people safer

img.cap: Long exposure of Panther beach off of Highway 1 just north of Santa Cruz. Photograph: Gary Qian/Getty Images

p: Panther state beach in California looks like something out of a dream: it lies among the coastal coves between Santa Cruz and Half Moon Bay, open directly to the Pacific. Dramatic shale cliffs climb 50ft into the air, while tiny pocket beaches sit between them, pummeled by large waves.
In this wild-seeming place, young people flock to escape city life: take pictures, build fires, and have colorful adventures that drip from postcards and Instagram carousels.

Recently, those happy moments have turned to horror. In the past six months, four young people have died at the beach. One fell off a bluff. One was knocked off the rocks and later died in the hospital. Two were swept off the beach while napping. A fifth is still missing after she was swept into the ocean.

That woman, 24-year-old Se Nah Park, walked to a cove on the beach with friends to build a bonfire, sing songs and enjoy the evening. When darkness fell, she tried to cross the beach again through a large “keyhole” archway that the beach is known for, but powerful waves knocked her down and carried her out to sea. Her father, Kwanghyon Park, asked anyone in the area to continue to look for her. “Anyone who’s hiking or in the area, please keep your eyes open for our beloved Senah,” Park
. “Just pray for us.”

The emergencies have put a spotlight on beach safety up and down the coast – and what can be done when social media beckons people to wild places. This past year, stronger storms and higher tides due to El Niño are creating new hazards at the beach.

“People see the beauty and want to enjoy the beauty, but don’t understand the dangers that the beauty hides,” says Michael Horn, public information officer of CalFire, the agency that is tasked with responding to emergencies at Panther beach.

California state parks manages the area and posts warnings about rip currents, cold water, high tides, and the risk of being stranded, says Scott Sipes, California state parks operations superintendent who leads operations for the Santa Cruz division. Those signs are posted at access points and the highway parking area.
But people don’t always heed the warnings, and some are calling for more to be done. The
suggested in an interview posting a death count at the trailhead.

“The reality is, they can’t be putting up barbed wire around every bit of California coastline,” says Horn. “When it starts getting really popular due to social media or people sharing the information about how beautiful an area is, even if they barbed-wired up the entire thing, people would find a way to get there.”

Gary Griggs, a professor at University of California, Santa Cruz, knows the beach well. He has taken students on field trips there for more than five decades, to study the cliffsides’ geology – it’s one of the largest exposed sedimentary intrusions on the planet. Because of the unique geology, cracks and fractures are common in the cliffs, leading to caves, tunnels and arches.

Griggs has watched the area’s popularity grow with visitors over recent years, partly due to infrastructure upgrades: a paved parking area, new bathrooms and a coastline bike path that passes by the coast all make Panther beach more attractive. The coastline is also only 45 minutes from bustling Silicon Valley cities like San Jose and Palo Alto – attracting a younger, outdoorsy crowd.

“It’s one of these few beaches you can actually park your car and walk down to in two minutes, whereas in some of the similar places, you have to walk 20 minutes to get to the beach,” Griggs says. “It looks like a welcoming place.”
The problems come with high tides, when the waves come right up to the cliff, erasing any sandy beach – particularly in the winter months. This year, a super El Niño has

Experts point out that El Niño isn’t solely to blame; rather the conditions have amplified existing dangers that have long existed at the beach. The region has seen at least

recorded since 2021, according to an analysis by a local reporter. CalFire’s Horn says that these sad events would happen even without the impacts of higher seas and higher tides. “I would honestly say my opinion is that this is 100% not El Niño-related,” he says, “because we get these kinds of incidents there all the time.”

A few years ago, a remote stretch of southern Oregon had problems with people getting injured at beaches – high surf and so-called sneaker waves would carry people away, and help couldn’t arrive for up to an hour after a call came in due to the remote location. Like in northern California, the rugged coastline has many coves, cliffs, and water that is cold, about 50F (10C) year-round. “You only have about 15 minutes before the body starts to have a hard time swimming on its own if you’re not wearing any type of flotation device,” says Luke Martinez, aquatic safety manager in Curry county, Oregon, and one of only two lifeguards patrolling about 100 miles (160km) of coastline.

Then, in 2020, Curry county came up with a plan to respond to rising tourism and the increase in beach incidents. When the National Weather Service issues a sneaker wave, high surf or related maritime warning, the lifeguard team fans out to beaches and talks to people, warning them in person about the risks. Martinez says they average more than 300 preventive contacts annually. And most importantly, there have been no south coast Oregon fatalities since the program began. Martinez says the team still does about a dozen rescues each year.

People are still taking risks: on 8 November, Martinez had just clocked off for the day when he got a call about a woman clinging to rocks in the dark on Secret beach, a well-known spot on the stretch of coast they patrol. He and his lifeguarding partner Shannon Ingram rushed to the beach and suited up. They found the woman swept 200ft (60 meters) down the coastline, where she was stranded on rocks roughly
offshore, in the pitch dark. The National Weather Service had issued a high surf warning for Oregon’s southern coast that day, forecasting breaking waves of 25 to 33ft.

Ingram reached the woman first and was able to secure her with a rescue tube and bring her back to shore. “The woman was super lucky,” Martinez says. “It could have been a lot worse – it wasn’t a good spot to be in. But things aligned so that we were able to get her out of there.”

Martinez says they are working with tourism organizations to include hazard information in visitor promotions – so that increasing tourism won’t mean more emergencies on the beach. “The ocean, even though it looks docile and weak at times, is always super powerful,” he says.

The best advice is to stay humble and keep situational awareness – and know that conditions can change quickly, says Horn. “The reality is, if the sand is wet, the ocean was there, and it’s going to come there again probably sooner than later,” he says.

There are lifeguards and park rangers talking to people at Panther beach and other wild beaches north of Santa Cruz, says Sipes. During the king tide event this week, the agency increased staffing to make those preventive contacts – but he also wants people to stay vigilant on wild, unlifeguarded beaches. “Understanding how to read the water and knowing the conditions before you go – those two actions are powerful things to keep people safe.”
